passage: The maths teacher wrote a fraction problem on the board and asked, “Any doubts?” Lalit's stomach turned over. He had not understood why the bottom numbers had to match, and the dozens of faces around him made the question feel enormous. Sarika, at the next desk, nodded as if she followed. If he asked, everyone would know he was slow. Lalit copied the problem into his notebook and looked at it hard, as though staring would help. That evening he tried the homework and got all six wrong, and the next day the tick marks were missing. The confusion, unspoken, had grown quietly like a weed behind a fence.

qa.q: How many homework problems did Lalit get wrong?
qa.a: Lalit got all six homework problems wrong.

qa.q: What was Lalit afraid of when the teacher asked for doubts?
qa.a: Lalit was afraid that everyone would know he was slow, so silence felt safer than asking.

qa.q: What could Lalit try before the next lesson so the confusion stops growing?
qa.a: Show the teacher the wrong homework quietly after class and ask the one thing he doesn't understand, why the bottom numbers must match.

qa.q: How might Sarika see Lalit's silence?
qa.a: Sarika probably sees only a quiet classmate, and does not know Lalit is lost; nodding along may also hide Sarika's own doubt.

grounding: A schoolchild sits confused and says nothing, afraid of looking stupid, so the confusion grows.

passage:
“Does anyone still not get it?” asked the science teacher, and twenty-eight heads stayed still.
Tejas leaned over. “Yogesh, do you get the food chain thing?”
“Yes. Easy,” said Yogesh, pen tight in his hand.
“Then what's a producer?”
“It's... um.”
“You don't know?”
“I do. I just can't say it,” muttered Yogesh, and stared at the desk. “Please don't ask Ma'am.”
“Why not?”
“Because everybody will laugh.”
At the end of the week the test paper came back with a red circle around the food chain question. Yogesh folded the paper very small and put it in his bag.

qa.q: How many heads stayed still when the teacher asked?
qa.a: Twenty-eight heads stayed still.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh ask Tejas not to ask Ma'am?
qa.a: Yogesh was afraid everybody would laugh, and felt embarrassed and shy about admitting confusion.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do before the next test to fix the food chain question?
qa.a: Ask Tejas or the teacher privately for a simple explanation of a producer and try it on a practice question.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel after being told “Please don't ask Ma'am”?
qa.a: Tejas is probably puzzled and a little worried for Yogesh, having offered a gentle question that got a tense answer.

grounding: A schoolchild pretends to understand rather than ask, because silence feels safer than exposure, and the confusion grows.

passage: The maths period had a substitute teacher, and Class 5 was noisier than usual. Trisha, ten, stared at the word problem about trains and could not tell what to multiply. Around her, everyone seemed to be writing. Her friend Minakshi was already on question three. Trisha's cheeks felt warm. If she asked, the substitute might say the answer loudly and everyone would turn. So she copied the question neatly, drew a small train, and waited. By the bell, she had solved nothing. At home, she cried a little over her notebook. Her father sat with her and asked what the problem said. She read it aloud, and together they found the multiplication.

qa.q: Why did Trisha stay silent instead of asking?
qa.a: She felt shy and afraid of looking stupid, worried that the substitute would say the answer loudly and everyone would turn.

qa.a: She could quietly ask Minakshi or write a note to the teacher, so she doesn't have to speak in front of the class.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have acted if she had known Trisha was stuck?
qa.a: Minakshi might have quietly explained the question, having understood it and sitting right there.

passage: In the Bengaluru school's science lab, Hafsa, nine, did not understand how to connect the bulb to the battery. The teacher had explained it once. Everyone else's bulbs were glowing. Hafsa held the wires and pretended to adjust them. Her classmate Lokesh leaned over. "Want help?" "No, I'm fine," she said quickly, her face hot. She didn't want him to think she was stupid. The period ended with her bulb still dark. At home she didn't mention it. In the next class, there was a quiz on circuits, and she left three questions blank. Afterwards, the teacher asked her to stay. "Hafsa, you can always ask me, even quietly." Hafsa nodded, eyes on the floor.

qa.q: What was Hafsa trying to connect?
qa.a: She was trying to connect the bulb to the battery.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa say she was fine when Lokesh offered help?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and afraid he would think she was stupid, so saying no felt safer.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond, and what else could help?
qa.a: The teacher kindly told her she can always ask, even quietly; a private signal or a note could make asking easier.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when Hafsa refuses his help?
qa.a: Lokesh might feel a bit confused or brushed off, since he was only trying to be kind.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild too embarrassed to ask for help, whose confusion grows until a quiz shows the gap.

Vaibhav: "Gurpreet, how was school?"
Gurpreet: "Fine."
Vaibhav: "And the fractions test next week? Are you ready?"
Gurpreet: (long pause) "I don't get fractions, Papa."
Vaibhav: "Since when?"
Gurpreet: "Since the first class. Everyone else understood."
Vaibhav: "Did you ask your teacher?"
Gurpreet: "No! Everyone would laugh. Aman already says I'm slow."
Vaibhav: "So you've been sitting there confused for two weeks?"
Gurpreet: (nods, eyes wet)
Vaibhav: "That sounds lonely. Thank you for telling me now. Shall we do one sum together tonight?"
Gurpreet: "Just one?"
Vaibhav: "Just one. And tomorrow, can you ask the teacher one question after class, when no one is around?"
Gurpreet: "Maybe."

qa.q: For how long had Gurpreet been confused about fractions?
qa.a: Gurpreet had been confused for two weeks, since the first class.

qa.q: Why hadn't Gurpreet asked the teacher?
qa.a: Gurpreet was afraid that everyone would laugh, especially since Aman already called Gurpreet slow.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do to help, and why could it work?
qa.a: He thanked Gurpreet, offered one sum together and suggested asking the teacher privately after class, which makes asking feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Vaibhav to learn of the two weeks of silence?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems concerned and gentle, recognising how lonely it must have been and choosing warmth over a lecture.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child who stayed silent for weeks out of fear of looking slow, and a parent making it safe to ask.

subtype: Child too shy or proud to ask [Actor]
passage: I'm Pooja. In class four we started long division, and on the first day I got lost at the step where you bring the next number down. Miss Thomas asked, "Everyone clear?" Lokesh, next to me, was already on sum three. I nodded. My ears went hot. I thought if I asked, the whole row would know I was the only one who didn't get it. The next day I copied the steps from the board without understanding them. By Friday there was a worksheet of ten sums, and I got two right. I hid it inside my atlas. Now I think the nod was the mistake. Every day I stayed quiet, the part I didn't understand got bigger.

qa.q: At which step of long division did Pooja get lost?
qa.a: At the step where you bring the next number down.

qa.q: Why did Pooja nod when Miss Thomas asked if everyone was clear?
qa.a: Pooja felt embarrassed and afraid of looking like the only one who didn't get it, which the hot ears show.

qa.q: What could Pooja try next time something is confusing?
qa.a: Pooja could ask Miss Thomas quietly after class, or write the question on a slip of paper, so nobody in the row has to hear.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had asked on the very first day?
qa.a: The confusion about one step could have been cleared in minutes, before it grew into a worksheet with only two right and a hidden sheet.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who stays silent over a confusing step for fear of looking stupid, so the confusion quietly grows.
